entries.sentence: The engine: the endless canvas, the exact editor, the cursor-centred view and the network that learns to use them.
A browser console where a person plays the editor through the agent's narrow view.
The brief, kept as written, and the discipline every experiment follows.
An exact memory kept from an earlier line: what the agent has seen, and nothing it has not.
The evidence of record: one directory per experiment, each with its dated account.
The exhibits: recorded episodes, films, stills, charts and the environment as a 3D model.
The scripted teacher copying a five-by-five grid of many colours, 114 clicks.
The teacher's episode as a particle tape, walked at the scale of a cell.
A learned agent copying a solid three-by-three square, 16 clicks.
Learning from reward alone: side 2 learned in three of three seeds, side 3 reads the colour and does not hand in.
A full-budget campaign across two machines; it has not finished and is not shown.
Imitation of the teacher at up to 87% per click, and why that still copies almost nothing.
The same recipe with a 'paint this cell this colour' vocabulary: 0 of 128.
The editor cut down to a world small enough to enumerate every state.
With the whole grid in view, a network learns the copy completely: 128 of 128 at three seeds.
The instruments: one script per experiment, and the ones that make these exhibits.
The checks that fail when a rule the engine relies on drifts.
Random play finds nothing in raw clicks and scores in over half its games in semantic actions.
Does a learner use one remembered glimpse? The bar was not met.
Does reward convert what imitation learned? Both arms 0 of 128.
Four credit-assignment levers, all 0 of 128.
Shuffling the teacher's painting order alone: 0 of 128 became 124 of 128.
Preconditions for reward learning: the submit gate and the step budget, measured before training.
The training harness had bugs the test suite missed; repaired and revalidated.
Remembering the source grid does not deliver its colours through the narrow view.
Closed-form ceilings on what the narrow view can support.
One remembered glimpse makes the many-coloured copy solvable in principle: the teacher solves 128 of 128.
